content: Methenamine is indicated for the prophylactic or suppressive treatment of frequently recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) when long-term therapy is deemed necessary. The recommended dosage for methenamine hippurate is 1 gram orally every 12 hours, while methenamine mandelate is dosed at 1 gram orally every 6 hours. In elderly patients, dose selection should be approached with caution, typically starting at the lower end of the dosing range. This is due to the increased likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. The combination of methenamine with acetazolamide is contraindicated because it may result in the formation of an insoluble precipitate in the urine, thereby reducing the efficacy of both agents. Similarly, methenamine should not be co-administered with sulfonamides such as sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, or sulfisoxazole, as these combinations can also lead to the formation of insoluble urinary precipitates, diminishing the therapeutic effects of both drugs. Methenamine and the cholera vaccine exhibit pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics, including methenamine, may interfere with the vaccine strain, reducing its efficacy. Therefore, the cholera vaccine should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Alternative therapies should be considered in such cases. Methenamine may decrease the effects of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Oral microbiota products contain bacterial spores, and the concurrent use of antibacterial agents can reduce their efficacy. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Methenamine may also reduce the effects of pseudoephedrine through an unknown mechanism. Urinary acidifying agents, such as methenamine, can increase the urinary excretion of indirect-acting alpha/beta agonists like pseudoephedrine, leading to lower serum concentrations. Caution and close monitoring are advised when these agents are used together. The co-administration of methenamine with sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid may reduce the efficacy of the latter by altering colonic bacterial flora, which is necessary for the conversion of sodium picosulfate into its active form. This interaction warrants caution and monitoring, and alternative therapies should be considered if necessary. Methenamine is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to methenamine or tartrazine (FD&C Yellow No. 5). It may cause adverse effects such as dysuria, gastric upset, nausea, rash, or hypersensitivity reactions. Liver function tests (LFTs) should be monitored, particularly in patients with a history of liver impairment. Methenamine use during pregnancy has not been established as safe, especially during the first and second trimesters, and it is classified as Pregnancy Category C. It may precipitate uric acid stones in patients with gout. Methenamine is excreted in breast milk, but no adverse effects have been documented in lactating mothers. Approximately 90% of methenamine is excreted in the urine within 24 hours. Mandelic or hippuric acid, the metabolites of methenamine, may accumulate in patients with severe renal impairment.
